subject: chemistry
title: Chemical bonds and types of structure
key_idea: There are three types of strong chemical bond: ionic, covalent and metallic. The bonding in a substance decides its structure, and the structure decides its properties. Metals with non-metals are ionic, non-metals with non-metals are covalent, and metals are metallic.

blocks.text: Every substance is held together by one of three strong bonds. This section covers what each one is and which elements form it.

items.meaning: The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed when electrons are transferred.
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms.
The attraction between metal ions and delocalised electrons.

rows: Compounds of a metal with a non-metal
Atoms that share pairs of electrons
Most non-metal elements and compounds of non-metals

items: Ionic bonding: a metal with a non-metal, with electrons transferred.
Covalent bonding: non-metal atoms sharing pairs of electrons.
Metallic bonding: metal atoms sharing delocalised electrons.

blocks.text: Bonding gives four main types of structure. Their properties follow from the bonds and how the particles are arranged.

items: Ionic and metallic substances have strong forces between their particles, so a lot of energy is needed to melt them.
Giant covalent substances have many strong covalent bonds to break.
Simple molecular substances have only weak forces **between** molecules, so they melt and boil easily. The covalent bonds inside the molecules do not break.
Ions can carry charge only when they are free to move, which is when an ionic compound is molten or dissolved.
Metals conduct because their delocalised electrons can move.

blocks.text: Atoms themselves do not have these bulk properties. A single atom or molecule has no melting point.

items: The type of bonding and structure explains the properties.
Simple molecules: weak forces between molecules, so low melting and boiling points.
Ionic, giant covalent and metallic: strong forces or bonds throughout, so high melting points.

sections.heading: Models of bonding and their limits

blocks.text: Diagrams and models show bonding, but every one leaves something out. This section covers what each model shows and what it hides.

rows: Which atom each outer electron comes from
The shape of the molecule or the size of the atoms
The 3D arrangement of atoms, and single or double bonds
The electrons, or the true size and spacing of the atoms
How much space the atoms fill
The atoms and bonds on a flat page

items: No single model shows everything about a structure.
A ball and stick model shows single and double bonds, but not the electrons.

checks.q: Name the type of bonding in a compound of a metal and a non-metal.
Ammonia, NH₃, boils at -33 °C. Silicon dioxide, SiO₂, boils at 2230 °C. Explain the difference.
checks.a: Ammonia is simple molecular with weak forces between molecules, which need little energy to overcome. Silicon dioxide is giant covalent with many strong covalent bonds, which need much more energy to break.

checks.q: A solid melts at 1085 °C, conducts electricity and is insoluble in water. Name its structure and bonding.
checks.a: Metallic: a giant structure of metal ions and delocalised electrons.

worked_example.question: Magnesium oxide is a compound formed from the metal magnesium and the non-metal oxygen. Describe what happens when a magnesium atom reacts with an oxygen atom. You should refer to electrons in your answer.
answer_points: Magnesium ions and oxide ions are formed, Mg²⁺ and O²⁻.
worked_example.tip: One mark each. Say how many electrons are transferred.

worked_example.question: Ammonia, NH₃, and silicon dioxide, SiO₂, are both compounds that are made of two non-metallic elements. Ammonia has a boiling point of -33 °C. Silicon dioxide has a boiling point of 2230 °C. Explain why the boiling points of ammonia and silicon dioxide are so different.
answer_points: Ammonia is simple molecular and has weak intermolecular forces.
Silicon dioxide is giant covalent and has strong covalent bonds.
More energy is needed to break the bonds in silicon dioxide than the intermolecular forces in ammonia.
worked_example.tip: Each point is marked independently. Name the structure and what is broken for both substances.

worked_example.question: The table shows some information about three different substances. Substance J: melting point 734 °C, boiling point 1435 °C, conducts electricity when molten or in solution. Substance K: melting point -182 °C, boiling point -162 °C, does not conduct electricity. Substance L: melting point 3422 °C, boiling point 5930 °C, conducts electricity. Substance L is also malleable. Identify the type of structure and bonding in each substance. Explain the properties shown in the table for each substance in terms of the type of structure and bonding.
answer_points: J is ionic. It has a high melting point because strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions take lots of energy to overcome.
J conducts only when molten or in solution, because the ions can then move. They cannot move when solid.
K is simple covalent. It has a low melting point because the weak intermolecular forces need little energy to overcome.
K does not conduct because it has no ions or delocalised electrons that can move.
L is metallic. It has a high melting point because of strong electrostatic forces between metal ions and delocalised electrons.
L conducts because its delocalised electrons can move.
worked_example.tip: A six-mark question is marked by level. Identify all three structures, then explain each property with a clear line of reasoning.
